summary: Adds SDC's comments to the discussion of network graphics protocols, with suggestions for supporting data-tablet input devices. It includes the usual disclaimer about ARPA funding and views.

plainLanguage.summary: A lab adds its ideas about how drawing tablets should work in the shared picture plan.

questions: how should a network handle data tablets
what did sdc suggest for graphics protocols
how should networks handle data tablets
what are the four data-tablet input types
subtitle: How drawing tablets should work over the network

tldr.problem: Early network systems lacked a standard way to transmit input from data-tablet drawing devices, which produce streams of X, Y, Z coordinates rather than simple text.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 199 proposes four message formats to handle tablet input: single-shot points, raw asynchronous data with variable timing, raw synchronous data with clock pulses, and preprocessed data that has been smoothed or filtered at the source.
tldr.outcome: The RFC did not become a standard, but it documented design ideas that influenced later network graphics protocols.

today: This 1971 proposal for network tablet input did not become a standard. The interactive graphics protocols that eventually emerged took different approaches. However, the RFC's ideas about preprocessing, filtering and communicating sampling rates influenced later work.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 199 adds SDC (System Development Corporation) comments to the discussion of network graphics protocols. It focuses on two areas: non-interactive graphics (like charts and graphs sent to display only) and data-tablet graphics (capturing hand-drawn input).

The RFC argues that protocol design should start with the simpler non-interactive case and add interactive features as extensions, rather than the other way around. This keeps the simple case simple and avoids forcing unnecessary complexity on basic users.
sections.plainLanguage: A lab said: start with simple pictures, then add fancy interactive ones later. Do not make simple pictures complicated just to support fancy ones.

sections.title: Data-Tablet Input Formats
sections.content:
A data-tablet generates input as coordinates: X and Y position on the writing surface (each to 1024 levels) and Z indicating pen contact. Input timing varies: single-shot sends one point per stroke, asynchronous sends points on demand as the pen moves, and synchronous sends points on a clock pulse.

RFC 199 proposes four formats. Single-shot: one coordinate pair per message. Raw asynchronous: a stroke as first point followed by delta X and delta Y for subsequent points. Raw synchronous: adds a sampling rate and sends a fixed number of points per stroke. Preprocessed: adds metadata like window size, minimum and maximum coordinates, and optional point counts for velocity estimation.
sections.plainLanguage: Four types of messages carry pen input: a single dot, a bunch of dots when the pen moves, dots sent on a timer, or processed dots with extra numbers about speed and size.

sections.title: Preprocessing and Character Display
sections.content:
Raw tablet data is noisy and voluminous. Preprocessing applies smoothing (such as an 8-point moving average) and filtering (removing redundant points within a window). The RFC specifies that filter windows can be square, rectangular, diamond or circular, and that both the smoothing and filter settings must be communicated in the protocol so the receiver knows what transformations were applied.

The RFC also addresses character generation for display. It proposes specifying character size, aspect ratio, and position with baseline alignment. Character prototypes are drawn on a 5 inch by 7 inch grid, and X and Y multipliers let the receiver scale them.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, the tablet can smooth out jitter and skip repetitive dots. The receiver needs to know what was done. Letters can be stretched or shrunk to fit.
